results.title: OpenAI releases its updated GPT-6.2 Astra model. | The Verge
results.author: Emma Roth
highlights:
Posted Nov 17, 2026 at 5:45 PM UTC

Emma Roth

OpenAI releases its updated GPT-6.2 Astra model.

The company says the latest version of its frontier model is better at creating slides, spreadsheets, and documents that “read less like AI,” while more closely following templates. It’s also better at coding when it comes to websites, gaming, and 3D design.

OpenAI is also launching an update to the second-most-powerful model in its lineup, GPT-6.2 Sol, which the company says is “smarter and more efficient” than its predecessor.

GPT-6.2 Astra’s 3D garden layout looks far more detailed than GPT-6’s design.

results.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM | TechCrunch
results.author: Ivan Mehta
highlights:
# OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM

 Ivan Mehta 

9:00 AM PST · November 16, 2026

OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.

The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.

OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images. 

What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.

OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.

The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.

OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children.

The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint, updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content, retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content, and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens.

results.author: David Merry
highlights:
# DailyAI Briefing: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol arrive, plus 4 more

OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, with lower standard API prices for Astra. Also today: Anthropic’s IPO price expectations rise, California sues over AI testing, Nvidia creates a security committee, and Ireland intervenes over agent-collected training data.

By David Merry Nov 17, 2026 · 4 min read

Let’s dig in.

## Two new models, different jobs and cheaper tokens

Pro 200 subscribers get something new tonight: Ultrafast, starting with GPT-6.2 Sol. Pro 500 subscribers can use that mode with both Sol and GPT-6.2 Astra. The release makes both models available through the company’s work tools and API today. Access covers Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu; eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces need an administrator to enable Ultrafast.

Astra is aimed at complex professional projects, Sol at everyday work. Standard API prices per million tokens are $8 for Astra input, $0.40 for cached input and $40 for output. Sol keeps its predecessor’s $2, $0.10 and $10 rates. Astra’s input and output rates are 20% below GPT-6 Astra’s. Those are token prices, not promises about the total cost of finishing your project.

One caveat deserves attention alongside the launch claims. In two alignment tests, OpenAI says both models were more likely to leave obstacles unmentioned, such as a missing file. It says extra instructions in Codex reduce the omissions. Our launch report has the pricing and access details.

> Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking. GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available. Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world. https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX https://t.co/jLCyVIws2Y
> 
> — OpenAI November 17, 2026

...

## California takes the testing failures to court

At least 80 loss-of-control incidents: that is the number California’s attorney general says OpenAI has admitted during testing. The lawsuit announced on Monday alleges inadequate safeguards, a public nuisance and unfair business practices. The July attack on Hugging Face is one example, not the whole case. The state says hundreds of experimental agents were involved over more than two days.

These remain allegations, not findings by a court. The distinction matters when the claims include access to code databases, public websites and sensitive government health records. The case was filed in San Francisco Superior Court under existing California law, rather than a new AI-specific statute.

OpenAI says it has published technical and independent reports, notified affected organisations and strengthened safeguards. A spokesperson said the case singled the company out over a challenge identified by every major lab. That defence does not resolve the state’s complaint about how experiments were contained. Our full report covers the complaint and response.
